name: Fatima Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, governments or political parties. We don’t sell anything or campaign, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My team coordinates product launches for a large company that licenses cartoon characters and music for other firms to use on their goods. I'm 43, with an MBA, and I lead sixteen coordinators; I'm paid near the top of the local range because I spot when a launch date and a contract don't agree. My partner makes fitted cabinets, our daughters are seven and fifteen, and our mortgaged home costs less than we could have borrowed for, so we've built 122,400 in cash, eighteen months of our 6,800 monthly spending. I use approved AI now and then for a meeting outline, after another manager has shown me it works, but I still check every date myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we should use whatever saves a few minutes and stop building every meeting around AI. A quiet launch with the right character on the right box is worth more than another demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel secure about our living in this picture. My 7,900 take-home and my partner's 2,100 cover our 6,800 monthly spending, including annual bills and the mortgage, and the reserve is separate. There are many similar management employers nearby if an ordinary company problem arises. I'd be content to let the excitement go past me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekly launch checks and use the approved outline tool only when it already saves me time. At home we'd continue our existing 3,200 monthly savings transfer and the normal mortgage payment throughout the first year. I wouldn't replace a working laptop or book a course for fear of missing the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with room in my head for something other than the next work announcement. I'd probably remember where I put the seeds for the balcony pots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on a supposedly quiet launch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the contract allows that character on that product in the month we've put on the shipping sheet. It's a small line in a long document, and getting it wrong means a lot of boxes sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop using the outline tool if AI disappointed generally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep it for the small job it does well. I don't need a tool to change civilisation before it can help me organise a meeting.

say: I'd tell the team to use **small time savings** without making AI the subject of every meeting.
I value a **quiet launch** with the right character on the right product.
think: I feel **financially secure**, with two incomes covering costs and a separate reserve.
I have **local options** if an ordinary company problem arises and can let the excitement pass.
do: Keep **weekly launch checks** and occasional approved outline-tool use when it saves time.
Continue the existing **3,200 monthly** savings transfer and ordinary mortgage payment through the first year.
feel: **Calm and mentally freer**, with attention left for home interests.
S0.quote: I don't need a tool to change civilisation before it can help me organise a meeting.
fieldNote: Her **selective use** of AI is established and practical, consistent with waiting until another manager demonstrates value.
Her **security** comes from a reserve, current surplus and local options, rather than assuming all management work is safe.

steps.text: Continue weekly launch checks and occasional approved meeting outlines
Continue the existing 3,200 monthly savings transfer and mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should measure a launch all the way through, not just how fast the first draft appears. If planning and checking take fewer people, I'd want the company to explain that before asking everyone to celebrate saved minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose part of my role because planning, checking contracts and coordinating dates are most of it. Being the person who spots a mismatch is valuable now, but software might do that checking better. Our finances leave room to adjust; they don't persuade me that my own post is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my director for two paid hours a week for six weeks with the experienced manager who already uses our approved planning tool. I'd start only after written agreement on those hours and permission to use cleared launch records, with no personal fee or unpaid catch-up work assumed. In the first year of change I'd use that time to learn the tool and compare its dates with completed launches, if approved; otherwise I'd continue the current process and seek another approved training date. I'd also join the existing staff forum's monthly lunchtime meeting to ask for published staffing plans, without treating an invitation as a guaranteed new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my role, but not rushed into buying a course. I feel better when I can name a small test and the point where I would stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as the test failing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A launch date that ignores a contract restriction, or time spent correcting the output that exceeds the saving. I'd record that as a failed use, not quietly repair everything and report a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you attend the staff meeting on paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's during my normal unpaid lunch, and I'd bring food from home as usual. I wouldn't call that employer-funded training or assume permission to miss a customer call outside the break.

say: I'd measure the **whole launch**, including corrections, rather than celebrate a faster first draft.
I'd ask for **staffing explanations** before treating saved minutes as a shared benefit.
think: I could lose **part of my role** because planning, contract checks and date coordination dominate it.
Our **financial room** helps adjustment but doesn't make my own post safe.
do: Request **twelve paid hours** over six weeks; start only with written time approval and cleared-record permission, without fees or assumed unpaid catch-up.
Compare **planning-tool dates** with completed launches if approved; otherwise continue current methods and request another approved training date.
Attend the **staff forum** during unpaid lunch to request published staffing plans.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, preferring a bounded test over a rushed purchase.
S1.quote: Our finances leave room to adjust; they don't persuade me that my own post is safe.
fieldNote: Her **learning request** has explicit paid hours, record permission and a fallback if approval is refused.
The **staff forum** uses unpaid lunchtime, while the trial records failures instead of turning hidden corrections into claimed success.

steps.text: Request twelve approved paid hours and cleared records before learning the planning tool
Attend lunchtime staff forum meetings and request published staffing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work that a launch coordinator isn't protected just because the customers still sell physical boxes. The thinking about contracts, dates and products could be done cheaply in 2028, before robots start moving those boxes around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my salary to go around 2028, and I'd feel the loss, although we wouldn't face an immediate cash emergency. My partner's cabinet work might keep earning for a while, but I wouldn't assume it survives the 2031 robots or even a weak order book before then. The reserve gives me control over the next decision, not a replacement career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the planned 18,000 kitchen refurbishment now, before we sign any contract; that money is still inside our 122,400 reserve. I'd keep working while the salary lasted, and in the first year after AGI I'd allow myself a six-month job search funded from cash if my post ended. With current spending and my partner's 2,100 wage the gap is 4,700 monthly, so I'd cap those six months' draws at 28,200 and review after three months; if his wage also stopped, we'd recalculate immediately rather than keep the same plan. I'd apply to actual advertised roles during that period, including lower paid ones, but wouldn't accept until a written offer and revised household budget showed we could fund the remaining shortfall for at least twelve months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to make a list rather than panic. I'd miss having my own salary more than I would miss the new kitchen doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the local management vacancies reassure you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if they were actual offers with work still to be done, and even then I'd regard a desk job as temporary. Many employers nearby doesn't mean many jobs protected from the same thinking machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when you reach the six-month search limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look at the remaining cash and spending before agreeing another period, rather than let six months become two years unnoticed. I wouldn't assume a benefit, a leaving payment or my partner's next wage had arrived until it actually had.

say: I'd explain that **physical products** don't protect the thinking work of launch coordination.
I'd distinguish **2028 desk exposure** from robots moving boxes around 2031.
think: I expect my **salary** to go around 2028 but don't foresee an immediate cash emergency.
The **reserve** gives decision time, while my partner's cabinet income and any replacement career remain uncertain.
do: Cancel the uncontracted **18,000 refurbishment**, keeping the money within the existing reserve.
Fund **six search months** after job loss, capped at 28,200 with partner income unchanged; review halfway or immediately if it stops.
Apply for **advertised roles**; accept only written offers whose revised budget funds any remaining shortfall for at least twelve months.
feel: **Anxious but organised**, expecting to miss her own salary more than the cancelled kitchen.
S2.quote: I'd miss having my own salary more than I would miss the new kitchen doors.
fieldNote: Her **search budget** uses a stated wage assumption and reserve draw cap, with an immediate review if the other wage stops.
She distinguishes **applications and acceptance**, requiring written terms and a funded household budget rather than treating local vacancies as safe earnings.

steps.text: Apply to advertised roles, accepting only written offers meeting the twelve-month funded-shortfall budget gate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us examine something before we put money into it. I'd support more shared ownership locally, but I wouldn't tell colleagues that a cooperative escapes the economics everyone else faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect the launch job to go around 2031, and another office qualification doesn't look like protection from almost any thinking work being cheap. I'd like some connection to work that isn't just another chain of launches, but that desire isn't proof of demand. I'd be anxious about wasting our preparation years on an attractive story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job now and ask the member-owned tool-hire shop near our house for its last three years of accounts and membership terms. I'd spend two Saturdays observing only if the shop agreed and our family calendar allowed, with no payment to me and no assumption of employment. I'd consider a membership investment of at most 4,000 only after an independent accountant checked the accounts for a fee capped at 600, both costs coming from new monthly surplus while our existing 122,400 reserve stayed untouched. In the first year after AGI, if those conditions weren't met I'd invest nothing; if I had joined, I'd keep its possible dividends at zero in the household budget and search for paid work after any launch-job loss, knowing robots around 2034 could also change the shop's physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a little interest returning when I picture seeing the shop's real books. I don't want the word community to become permission to stop checking the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop won't share the accounts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't buy a membership stake, however friendly the people are. I can still wish them well without handing over money on the strength of a pleasant Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you buying yourself a job there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, membership doesn't come with wages, a shift or authority to make decisions alone. If a paid vacancy appeared I'd apply separately, and I wouldn't count its income before an accepted written offer.

say: I'd support **shared ownership** while warning that a cooperative still faces the same economic changes.
I'd tell colleagues that **five years** allows checking before spending.
think: I expect the **launch job** to go around 2031 without another office qualification protecting it.
I want a different **work connection**, but fear wasting preparation years on a story without demand.
do: Request **three years' accounts** and observe two Saturdays only with shop agreement and space in the family calendar, without pay.
Invest at most **4,000** only after an accountant's check costing at most 600, funded from new surplus with 122,400 untouched.
Budget **zero dividends** if invested; otherwise invest nothing, and seek paid work separately after launch-job loss.
feel: **Anxious but interested**, determined that community language must not replace checking the sums.
S3.quote: I don't want the word community to become permission to stop checking the sums.
fieldNote: The **investment enquiry** is not a job offer; observation, paid accounting advice and any stake have separate gates.
Her **reserve** stays protected, dividends are budgeted at zero and she recognises the cooperative's later robot exposure.

steps.text: Request tool-hire cooperative accounts and permission for two unpaid observation Saturdays
Consider a stake up to 4,000 after a check up to 600, protecting the reserve
Seek paid work separately after launch-job loss without assuming cooperative wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to give children choices without pretending to know which job titles will survive. I'd back public training support that adults can use more than once, because guessing right at sixteen shouldn't decide the next forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and still expect to lose launch-management pay, but I wouldn't feel as pressed as in the two-year picture. Our daughters would be seventeen and twenty-five, so the expensive years wouldn't all arrive together. My partner's cabinet work might also change radically with robots around 2039, and I wouldn't call either of us retired without seeing how the money lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd separate 12,000 of our current reserve into an education account for the daughters, leaving 110,400 accessible for household shocks; I'd tell them that's a limited contribution, not a promise to cover everything. We'd review actual course fees and living costs with each daughter before paying anything, without choosing a subject on a forecast of safe jobs. I'd write to our elected representative for repeatable adult training support during the preparation years. In the first year after AGI, if my pay ended, we'd pause further education gifts beyond that 12,000 and review the actual reserve and my partner's wage every quarter before agreeing more spending or training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the wage eventually, but less hurried and more generous in how I can think about the children. I'd rather promise my daughters a bounded amount of help than a safe occupation I can't name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the education money if household income fell earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd tell the daughters before making a payment that their account still belongs to us until fees are paid. If essentials couldn't be covered from the household reserve, we'd reconsider the education contribution together rather than borrow to keep a promise we could no longer afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain just because public funding became available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still need the actual course, covered fees, timetable and a reason to attend. Public support would widen a choice; it wouldn't oblige me to buy the first claim about guaranteed work.

say: I'd tell families to give children **choices** without claiming to know which job titles survive.
I'd support **repeatable adult training** so one teenage decision doesn't determine a lifetime.
think: At **53**, I expect my launch salary to end but feel less pressed than with 2028.
Our daughters' **different ages** spread costs, while my partner's later robot exposure prevents an assumption of funded retirement.
do: Set aside **12,000 for education**, leaving 110,400 for household shocks; reconsider unpaid contributions if essentials aren't covered.
Check actual **fees and living costs** before payments, without choosing subjects from safe-job forecasts.
Write for **repeatable training support** and review household money quarterly after salary loss before further gifts or training.
feel: **Anxious but less hurried**, able to think more generously about her daughters' choices.
S4.quote: I'd rather promise my daughters a bounded amount of help than a safe occupation I can't name.
fieldNote: Her **education allocation** has a cash amount, payment checks and an explicit essentials-first condition before money is committed.
She separates **public support** from a decision to train and never treats available funding as proof of guaranteed employment.

steps.text: Earmark 12,000 for daughters education, reconsidering unpaid contributions if household essentials lack funding
Write to her elected representative requesting repeatable adult training support
Review actual household money quarterly after salary loss before further gifts or training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because losing a salary with almost no warning would force decisions faster than I like to make them. A dated account of what the company plans, portable training support with actual fees covered, and clear access to income support would help. Savings buy us thinking time, and I'd like other families to have some too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people won't spend money on. I won't buy an expensive qualification because somebody prints a shortage forecast on the brochure. I learned to wait for evidence after my first employer closed a division everyone had called essential.

headlineQuote: Savings buy us thinking time, and I'd like other families to have some too.
portrait: Fatima is **43**, an MBA manager paid near the top of the local range for coordinating complex licensed-product launches.
She has **two daughters**, a cabinetmaker partner, a mortgage and eighteen months of current household spending in cash.
She uses **AI occasionally**, following proven examples and checking dates rather than volunteering for each new system.
Her **evidence-first approach** shapes training, a possible cooperative investment and family education choices without promising permanent protection from AGI.
biggestWorry: I fear **AGI by 2028** most because sudden salary loss would force decisions faster than I prefer.
whatWouldHelp: I need **dated company plans**, portable training support covering real fees and clear access to income support.
